articles.title: Orca Security adds visibility into AI-generated code and agent risks
articles.context: Expand security coverage across AI development platforms: Turn discovered services into actionable security coverage through supported integrations and posture assessments,...
articles.full_text:
Orca Security has announced new capabilities to help organizations discover and secure AI-generated applications and autonomous agents across their cloud environments. The expansion builds on Orca’s AI Security offering, enabling security teams to uncover previously unknown AI applications, assess the risks associated with autonomous agents, and gain deeper visibility into AI-generated code.

AI is fundamentally changing who builds software and how it reaches production. Employees across business functions are creating applications using AI-powered tools, while developers increasingly rely on autonomous agents to write code and execute tasks. Yet many of these applications and agents operate outside traditional security processes, creating new blind spots.

“AI has turned everyone into a builder, but security teams are often the last to know what’s been created,” said Gil Geron, CEO of Orca Security. “An employee can deploy an application over the weekend, while an autonomous agent can access sensitive data and take actions across cloud environments. Organizations need to understand not just what exists, but what it can access and where it creates risk. We’re bringing that context to the entire AI development ecosystem so companies can keep innovating without losing control.”

Uncovering shadow AI applications through digital fingerprints

As employees increasingly use AI development platforms such as Lovable, Replit, and Bolt to create applications outside traditional engineering workflows, security teams often lack visibility into what has been deployed, where it runs, or what company data it can access. Traditional discovery approaches depend on knowing which platforms, applications, or repositories to monitor, leaving unknown AI-generated applications undetected.

Orca’s expanded AI AppGen Security capabilities address this challenge by identifying digital fingerprints that AI application builders leave behind across cloud infrastructure, DNS records, workloads, code repositories, and cloud identities. Using its patented agentless SideScanning technology and unified data model, Orca connects these signals to uncover previously unknown AI services without requiring additional agents, vendor integrations, or employee registration.

New capabilities allow users to:

Discover shadow AI applications through service fingerprints: Automatically detect digital fingerprints left behind by AI application builders such as Lovable, v0, Replit, Base44, and Bolt, alongside hosting and data services including Vercel, Netlify, and Supabase. Orca identifies evidence such as DNS records pointing to builder infrastructure, installed packages, file markers, AI builder commit identities, and cloud permissions, revealing services that security teams may not know are in use.

Connect fingerprints to business risk: Correlate discovered services with cloud identities, IAM permissions, and accessible resources to help security teams understand which AI-generated applications may have access to sensitive company data. Findings are presented through a dedicated Service Fingerprints view, asset-level details, and an AI AppGen dashboard, providing the evidence behind each discovery.

Expand security coverage across AI development platforms: Turn discovered services into actionable security coverage through supported integrations and posture assessments, including checks for insecure configurations such as disabled row-level security in Supabase projects. Orca is also extending AI AppGen Security support to Base44, OpenAI, and Vercel.

“Many organizations still struggle to discover what’s been built and where it runs. Now that building is no longer confined to engineering, discovery has to start from what these AI-generated apps leave behind in the environment, not from the builder declaring anything,” said Grace Trinidad, Research Director, IDC.

Securing autonomous AI agents and AI-generated code

Beyond AI-generated applications, autonomous agents introduce a new category of security risk. Unlike traditional AI models, agents can execute commands, access sensitive information, and interact with enterprise systems using the credentials and permissions available to them. A single overprivileged agent or insecure connection can create a path to sensitive data or critical infrastructure.

Orca’s expanded AI agent security posture capabilities provide visibility into cloud-managed and self-hosted agents, including coding agents operating on cloud infrastructure. By incorporating agents into its unified data model and existing cloud security workflows, Orca enables organizations to:

Discover and inventory AI agents: Automatically identify cloud-managed and self-hosted agents, including coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI running on cloud workloads. A new Agents tab in Orca’s AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) provides a centralized inventory alongside AI models, packages, and MCP servers, with filtering by cloud, account, and framework.

Map agent relationships and access: Connect agents to the AI models they use, MCP servers and tools they interact with, cloud identities they operate under, and data stores they can access. This context helps security teams understand an agent’s potential blast radius and identify paths to sensitive data.

Detect and prioritize agent-specific risks: Identify agents with excessive permissions, disabled approval controls, exposed credentials in MCP configurations, insecure HTTP connections, or access to destructive tools. Findings are incorporated into Orca’s dynamic risk scoring and attack path analysis to prioritize the most consequential exposures and provide actionable remediation guidance.

Track and secure AI-generated code: Attribute code to the coding agents and AI models that produced it, helping organizations understand the proportion of AI-generated code across repositories and identify which agents and models contribute the most security risk. Through Orca’s AI Skills Hub, developers can also integrate security requirements, application security scanning, and remediation directly into coding agents before code is committed.

These capabilities extend Orca’s existing cloud security workflows to AI agents, enabling organizations to assess agent-related risks alongside vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, identities, and sensitive data across their environments.

articles.title: See Your Cloud and Coding AI Agents in Context
articles.context: When a prompt injection lands on an agent, the attacker inherits all of it
articles.full_text:
Securing AI in the cloud has historically meant securing models. Teams called Amazon Bedrock or Azure OpenAI, maybe hosted an open model on a GPU instance, and security’s job was to find those services, check their configurations, and keep training data from leaking.

AI Agents changed that. An agent takes the model’s output and acts on it. It calls tools, reads and writes data, opens tickets, runs code, and talks to other agents. To do any of that, it needs credentials and permissions. And in most organizations, nobody reviewed what those permissions are.

Orca now discovers the agents running in your cloud, both cloud-managed and self-hosted, including the coding agents your developers run on cloud infrastructure. The platform maps what each agent is connected to, and flags the agents that are misconfigured, over-privileged, or within reach of sensitive data.

Why are agents a different kind of AI risk?

A model’s risk is mostly about what it knows and what it says. An agent’s risk is about what it can do. That depends on four things that usually live in four different places:

The models it calls, managed or self-hosted.

The MCP servers it connects to, each exposing its own set of tools and running with its own credentials.

The identity it runs as, typically the IAM role or service account of the workload it lives on.

The data that identity can reach, from RAG sources and training buckets to production databases.

Agents also tend to blur identity lines. Many run under the same identity as the humans who use them, or inherit whatever role the host machine carries. When a prompt injection lands on an agent, the attacker inherits all of it.

You can’t assess an agent just by looking at the agent. You have to see everything it’s connected to.

Why do existing tools miss it?

Most AI security tools see one layer. One inventories models. Another watches prompts. A third scans code. None of them knows that the LangChain agent on an EC2 instance is authenticated to an MCP server holding a Jira API token, or that its instance role can read an S3 bucket full of customer records.

Consider two agents running in the same account:

Agent A connects to a read-only documentation MCP server. Its workload role can reach one internal bucket of public product docs.

Agent B is a coding agent on a CI runner, configured to bypass permission checks so it runs commands with no human approval. It connects to an MCP server whose environment carries a CI/CD API token, and that server exposes tools like delete_bucket_object and revoke_db_access. The runner’s instance role can read a database containing PII.

An inventory lists both as “AI agent.” Only context tells you that one is a low-risk helper and the other is a path to your crown jewels.

Three Ways Orca Delivers AI Agent Security Posture

#1: Inventory as part of the AIBOM

Orca builds one inventory of every AI agent in your cloud, whether your teams use a managed agent platform or build their own.

Every agent appears in a new Agents tab in the AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM), filterable by account, cloud and framework, with new Agents widgets on the AI Security dashboard. Because SideScanning reads workload data out-of-band, there is nothing to install. No agents are required to find your agents.

AIBOM in the Orca Platform covering models, packages, MCP servers, and AI Agents

#2: Clear relationships in the Unified Data Model

Orca models every agent as a first-class asset in its Unified Data Model and links it to the things that define its risk:

The AI models it uses.

The MCP servers it connects to, whether local or remote, and the tools each server exposes.

The AI packages it was built with.

The IAM role it runs as, and the data stores that role can access.

Because these relationships sit in the same graph as the rest of your cloud, an agent’s blast radius is a question you can answer directly: what can this agent touch, and what could an attacker do with it?

An agent inventory tells you what exists. Agent context tells you what’s at stake.

See an AI agent’s connections to models, IAM roles, data stores, and policies in the Orca Platform.

#3: Prioritized risk in context

Orca adds new alerts built for agent risk: misconfiguration, over-privilege, reachable sensitive data, and runtime detections. Findings include:

AI agents authenticated to MCP servers that hold credentials, such as Jira, Confluence or Jenkins API tokens. A prompt injection against that agent inherits whatever the credential can reach.

AI agents configured to bypass permission checks, which removes the human approval step before the agent reads files, runs commands or calls tools.

MCP configuration files containing live secrets. Orca matches the secret value itself, so a hardcoded token is flagged and a safe environment-variable reference is not.

MCP servers communicating over plaintext HTTP to remote endpoints, exposing tool calls and their data in transit.

MCP tool sets that grant destructive tools such as deleting data, revoking access or terminating clusters.

Each alert includes plain-language remediation steps and is scored with Orca’s dynamic risk scoring, which weighs reachability, exploitability and blast radius rather than a static severity label. Agents can also serve as points in Orca’s attack path analysis, so an over-privileged agent two hops from a production database ranks above a misconfigured agent with nothing nearby.

Use Orca to see what an AI agent can access.

What about the coding agents your developers use?

Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI don’t only run on laptops. Teams run them on CI runners, cloud dev environments and build servers, where they pick up the host’s cloud credentials. Orca detects coding agents on cloud workloads the same way it detects any self-hosted agent, including the MCP servers they connect to and settings that turn off their approval prompts.

Coding agents also leave a second footprint: the code they write. Orca attributes code to the AI coding agents and models that wrote it, so you can see what share of your codebase is AI-generated, which repositories carry the most risk in AI-written code, and which models are linked to the most alerts.

Track the risk contributions of Coding Agents to improve their quality.

Visibility is half the job. Through Orca’s AI Skills Hub, you can plug skills and hooks into coding agents so they pull your security requirements, run AppSec scans, and fix issues to policy before code is committed.

One unified platform for cloud and AI risk

Agent findings land in the same alert workflows, integrations and dashboards your team already uses for the rest of your cloud. There is no separate AI console and no separate severity scale. The question every security team now has, “what are our agents doing and what can they reach?”, gets answered with the same context Orca already applies to workloads, identities and data.

Orca shows you every AI agent in your cloud, what it’s connected to, and which ones put sensitive data at risk, so your team can fix the riskiest agents first without slowing down the teams building them.

Want to see which agents are running in your cloud and how far they can reach? Book a personalized demo.

articles.title: Shadow AI Generated Apps: Find Them in the Cloud and Code You Already Scan
articles.context: The Orca Research Pod recently found that 51% of organizations have adopted AI to build software, yet 81% have critical vulnerabilities in AI packages (Hacker Valley News, 2026)
articles.full_text:
The Orca Research Pod recently found that 51% of organizations have adopted AI to build software, yet 81% have critical vulnerabilities in AI packages (Hacker Valley News, 2026). In 2025, CVE-2025-48757 showed how a single missing database policy in AI-generated Supabase projects exposed data across more than 170 production apps.

None of these apps went through a pull request or a security review. People outside engineering built them, often over a weekend, from accounts the security team had never seen.

When we introduced AI AppGen Security, we made the case that AI app builders turned every employee into a builder, and that the platforms those apps run on need security built for how they work. We started with integrations for Claude Enterprise and Vercel.

The first question we heard from security teams: how do I connect a platform I don’t know we use? Nobody files a ticket for a budget-forecasting app built on Lovable, and the marketing team’s campaign portal never reached architecture review. You can’t connect what you’ve never heard of.

AI app builders leave fingerprints in the DNS, workloads, code, and cloud identities Orca already scans agentlessly. Orca now flags them, so you can find AI-built apps nobody told you about and see what data they can reach. Below, we walk through why your current tools miss these apps, how Orca finds them, and what to do once you know.

Why the usual discovery paths miss AI-generated apps

You’d expect at least one of your existing tools to catch these apps. Here’s why none of them do.

Secure web gateways and CASBs see the visit, not the app. They can tell you an employee opened Lovable or Replit. They can’t tell you what was deployed, what data it holds, or whether it requires a login.

SSPM sees sign-ups through your identity provider. It reads IdP logs and OAuth grants, which shows the SaaS your employees signed up for with a work email. An app built from a personal account never touches your IdP.

AppSec scans the repositories you point it at. If a builder’s bot created the repo in a workspace security has never seen, nobody points anything at it.

Cloud security sees the evidence but doesn’t connect it to the service. A CNAPP already inventories the DNS record, the IAM user, and the package on the VM. Until now, a subdomain resolving into a builder’s IP range was just an address, and an IAM user created by an app builder was just an IAM user. The data was there. Nothing tied it to the service behind it.

Every one of these tools waits for someone to connect a system, a user, or a repo first. The apps that matter most are the ones nobody connected to.

How does Orca find apps nobody reported?

Services that run outside your environment still leave traces inside it. Orca already scans your cloud accounts, workloads, repositories, and external attack surface, so the traces are already in its data.

A fingerprint is an observed trace that ties an asset you own to an external service. Orca stores each one in its unified data model, where you can query it like any other asset. Each one records the service, the type of evidence, the exact value that matched, and when Orca first saw it.

To find these fingerprints, there’s no new agent to deploy, no vendor API to authorize, and nothing for the builder to opt into. Here’s where the evidence comes from:

Your external attack surface. DNS records whose values point into a builder’s or host’s infrastructure, vendor domain-verification records, and response headers showing a site is set up to load inside a builder’s live editor.

Your workloads. SideScanning already inventories installed packages and reads files across VMs and container images. Some builder packages only work inside the builder’s own development environment, so if one shows up on a workload, the project started there. File markers matter as much as packages, because production builds often strip out dependency manifests. Without file markers, package inventory can come back empty on the very images running an AI-built app.

Your code repositories. When an AI builder writes code, it commits under its own bot identity. That identity survives every human edit that follows, so the commit author is the most reliable sign a builder was involved.

Your cloud identities. When an app builder or its host connects to your cloud, it leaves an identity behind: an IAM user or role it authenticates as, a trust policy that lets it in, and a permissions policy naming what it can read. It’s also the only source that tells you what company data the service can reach.

Orca matches what a record points to, not what it’s called. A subdomain named lovable-test that points to a private IP doesn’t get flagged, and an app hosted on Vercel isn’t counted as built with v0. A discovery screen that flags every string with a vendor name in it gets muted within a week.

What can security teams do with the results?

Finding the app is the first step. Next you need to know what it can touch, and get it covered.

Detect: see every AI app service in use, and the evidence behind each one. Findings appear in three places:

AI AppGen Fingerprints have a dedicated Service Fingerprints view grouped by service type and then by service.

On each asset’s page, every fingerprint on that asset is listed with the value that matched.

Dashboard widgets summarize what’s detected, what’s connected, and posture for connected services.

How to find AI-built apps in your cloud environment with Orca. People across a company ship apps with AI app builders such as Lovable, v0, Bolt and similar tools, often without security teams knowing. This demo shows how Orca finds these apps and what they can reach. AI app builders leave evidence in cloud environments, code and DNS. Orca detects these fingerprints from data it already scans, with no agent, vendor API or opt-in required. Fingerprints are grouped by service, and the demo shows fingerprints from Base44, Supabase, Lovable and other AI platforms. For services that Orca integrates with, connect the account to secure the AI platform the same way the cloud is secured: identify issues, prioritize risk and implement remediation. Drill into the asset where a fingerprint was detected to see which other AI app services are tied to it. Set up dashboard widgets to track the footprint of AI-built apps in the cloud environment and manage risk while enabling AI innovation across the business. The demo ends with an invitation to discover shadow AI platforms in the cloud and to contact the Orca team to get started.

Connect: turn a finding into coverage. Where Orca supports a platform you haven’t connected, the fingerprint comes with a Connect action. Detection shows you which connections are worth making. Connecting turns on posture checks inside the platform, like flagging Supabase projects with row-level security turned off.

Why the evidence matters more than the count. Picture two Lovable apps, both found by Orca on the same day:

A marketing landing page. It has a DNS record pointing at the builder and nothing else: no cloud identity and no access to company data.

An internal expense tracker. It has the same DNS record, plus an IAM user Lovable created in your AWS account, with a policy that can read a bucket of customer records.

A tool that counts apps tells you there are 2. What you need to know is that one of them can read customer data.

That’s why the cloud identity fingerprint matters most to a CISO. The policy attached to a builder’s identity has a Resource element that names the buckets, datasets, and query workgroups it can reach.

Finding the AI app builder is only half the answer. The other half is naming the crown jewels the AI-built app can read.

Fingerprints are findings, not alerts. They don’t open alerts or change an asset’s risk score. They give you an inventory to govern from: decide which AI app builders your company allows, then use the Service Fingerprints view to spot the ones you don’t.

One limit to know about: DNS fingerprints cover only the zones Orca can read. The dashboard shows whether your DNS provider is connected, so a zone Orca can’t see never looks clean.

Which services does Orca detect?

Orca fingerprints these services:

AI app builders: Lovable, Vercel, v0, Replit, Base44, Netlify, and Bolt

Data services: Supabase

Where Orca has integrations set up with these services, security teams can connect and secure those AI platforms.

Your builders will keep shipping apps nobody asked security about. Now you’ll know when they do, and what those apps can reach.

Want to see which AI app builders are already running in your environment? Request a demo and we’ll walk you through it.

About the Orca Platform

As cloud, applications, AI and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca transforms security risk into the context teams need to act. The Orca Platform provides complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, correlates risk across every layer, and prioritizes the exposures that matter most so organizations can remediate faster and innovate with confidence. articles.title: A Kubernetes CVE just dropped. Here’s how to find and fix what matters.
articles.context: ” Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access
articles.full_text:
Critical Kubernetes CVEs arrive constantly. Some hit an operator or controller, some the Linux kernel underneath your nodes, others the container images your teams ship every day. Each one comes with a CVSS score and an urgent recommendation to patch.

What it doesn’t come with is context. A CVSS score tells you how bad a flaw could be in theory. It can’t tell you whether the vulnerable component runs in your clusters, whether anyone could actually exploit it, or what it can reach. Without those answers, teams either scramble to patch everything at once or let the CVE sit in a backlog until it’s forgotten.

Kubernetes makes this harder than most environments. Workloads are ephemeral, permissions are spread across roles, bindings and service accounts, and a single foothold can travel from a pod to a node, from a node to the cloud account, or through a privileged operator to everything it manages.

This post walks through a repeatable approach for triaging any Kubernetes CVE in Orca, then puts it to work on a real example: Copy Fail, a Linux kernel flaw affecting nodes across nearly every major cloud and operating system.

How to triage a Kubernetes CVE: Four questions to ask

Whatever the CVE, effective triage comes down to the same four questions. Orca answers each one from a single platform for cloud security, across every cluster and the cloud accounts they run in.

Where does it run?

Is it internet exposed?

Is it exploitable?

What can it reach?

Each answer narrows the list for the next, so a CVE that touches dozens of clusters ends with a short, ranked set of actions. Here’s how that looks on a real example.

The example: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431)

Copy Fail is a bug in the Linux kernel that lets an ordinary user quietly give themselves full admin (root) access. In Kubernetes, that means an attacker who gets into any container can take over the node it runs on, and from there, potentially everything that node can reach. Here’s how Orca takes you from the headline to a fix.

Step 1: Find which nodes and images are affected

Orca’s emerging threats feed, From the News, flags Copy Fail with a plain-language summary and recommended fix. From there, search CVE-2026-31431 in the Vulnerabilities view, part of Orca’s agentless vulnerability management, to see every affected node, node pool and image across clusters and clouds, with the fixed kernel version for each.

Prefer plain English? Ask Orca AI, an AI reasoning engine for security teams, “Which Kubernetes nodes are affected by CVE-2026-31431?” and get the same answer in seconds.

Step 2: Check whether affected nodes or pods are internet exposed

Copy Fail needs a foothold inside a pod first, so checking the node alone isn’t enough. A node can sit on a private network and still run a pod that’s reachable from the internet through a LoadBalancer or an Ingress. If that pod is compromised, the attacker lands on the node’s kernel just the same. Click into an affected node to see its asset details, including whether the node or any workload running on it is publicly accessible, and how many high-severity risks it carries. Nodes with any internet-facing path go to the top of the list. Nodes with no exposure still get patched, just on a normal cycle.

Step 3: Confirm whether the CVE is exploitable

Open the Copy Fail risk on that node to see the vulnerable kernel package it affects, along with Orca’s exploitability and risk scoring details. Copy Fail has public exploit code, so the answer is yes, and on a node with an internet-exposed workload, that moves it from “patch soon” to “patch now.”

Step 4: Map the attack path from node to cloud

A node escape is only as dangerous as what the node can access. Use attack path analysis to see how an attacker could move to the cloud roles, secrets or crown jewel data within reach, all in one ranked path. That’s the alert you patch first.

Go further with Orca: Remediate, prevent, and prove progress

That’s the triage done. But finding the risk is only part of the job, and Orca helps with the rest too.

Prove progress to leadership. When leadership asks where things stand, you shouldn’t need to scramble and pull a spreadsheet together to answer. The K8s & Container Security dashboard shows how many clusters and nodes are still affected, and that number drops as patches roll out, so one view shows both your current risk and your progress.

Patch without letting new risk in. Teams keep deploying while patches roll out, and every new pod is a possible foothold. Orca’s Admission Controller checks each workload before it’s admitted, stopping new privileged or host-namespace pods, which make it easier to take over a node from a compromised container, from landing in affected clusters. Policies can warn or block depending on what you need, and every decision is logged in Orca alongside the CVE you’re tracking.

Stay audit-ready. An unpatched critical vulnerability is an audit finding waiting to happen. Orca automatically maps it to the regulatory compliance frameworks you report on, such as PCI DSS 4.0 and SOC 2, so you know which controls are affected now and have the evidence ready once remediation is done, instead of scrambling for it later.

Cut the time to fix. Orca opens tickets in tools you already use with the affected nodes and fixed kernel version already filled in, so engineers start fixing instead of investigating, and you can track every ticket through to closure. Where patching has to wait, disabling the affected kernel module is a quick interim mitigation.

Catch an attack before the patch lands. Rolling new images across a fleet takes time, and that window is when attackers move. Orca’s cloud detection and response monitors affected workloads for suspicious activity, so if someone tries to use the foothold, you know right away and can respond.

Together, that’s the difference between knowing about a CVE and being done with it.

A repeatable workflow for the next Kubernetes CVE

Kubernetes CVEs aren’t slowing down, and patching everything the moment it’s disclosed isn’t realistic. The teams that stay ahead are the ones that know where those CVEs are throughout their environment, and which ones need to get remediated first.

Orca helps you do exactly that. From the first alert to the closed ticket, the Orca Cloud Security Platform shows you where a CVE runs, whether it’s exposed, whether it’s exploitable, what it can reach, and how it affects your compliance posture. Copy Fail is one example. The same workflow works for whatever CVE lands next.

See it in your own environment. Request a demo and we’ll walk through how Orca triages the Kubernetes CVEs that matter most to your clusters. To go deeper on Orca’s Kubernetes and Container Security capabilities, download the data sheet.

articles.title: *sshole: OpenSSH Authentication Bypass Gives Attackers Root on Alpine Linux
articles.context: A critical authentication bypass, with no CVE assigned yet, was disclosed in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux distributions such as Alpine
articles.full_text:
A critical authentication bypass, with no CVE assigned yet, was disclosed in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux distributions such as Alpine. An unauthenticated attacker can log in over SSH password authentication as an account that should not accept passwords at all, including root. On a default Alpine install that means root access from a single connection, so patch now.

How the *sshole vulnerability bypasses SSH authentication

The bug comes from how musl libc’s crypt() reports errors. Since 2012, musl has returned the string “*” when crypt() fails instead of NULL, and its SHA-256 and SHA-512 crypt refuse passwords longer than 256 bytes. Locked and key-only accounts also use “*” as their shadow password field. When sshd checks passwords itself, without PAM, a password between 257 and 1024 bytes makes crypt() fail and return “*”. That matches the stored field, and sshd lets the attacker in.

Which locked and key-only accounts are exposed

Accounts exposed this way include root on Alpine 3.16 and later, key-only service and deploy users, directory users from nslcd, winbind or sssd, and the “alpine” user in tiny-cloud images, which has passwordless doas and is effectively root.

Which Alpine Linux and musl-based systems are affected

A system is affected when all of these hold: sshd is built without PAM (or runs with UsePAM no) on musl libc, PasswordAuthentication is on (the default), at least one account has “*” as its password field, and at least one local account has a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash. On Alpine that means the openssh-server package on releases 3.16 through 3.24 and edge. Other musl-based systems such as OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto builds, and container images that run sshd, may also be exposed. glibc distributions, PAM-enabled sshd, Dropbear and non-Linux systems are not affected.

How to patch *sshole: fixed OpenSSH versions and mitigations

Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2, or on Alpine to openssh 10.6_p2-r0 (edge), 10.3_p1-r2 (3.24), 10.2_p1-r1 (3.23), 10.0_p1-r11 (3.22), 9.9_p2-r1 (3.21) or 9.7_p1-r6 (3.20). Restart sshd afterwards, because upgrading the package does not replace the daemon that is already running. If you cannot patch yet, setting PasswordAuthentication no closes the hole. Also search authentication logs for “Accepted password for” on accounts that have no password, and treat any host with such a line as compromised.

Is *sshole being exploited in the wild?

The researcher’s public write-up explains the technique in enough detail to reproduce it, and no exploitation in the wild has been reported so far. Internet-facing Alpine hosts with password login enabled are the most exposed. An attacker who gets in this way has root on the host and can use it to reach the rest of the environment.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable OpenSSH hosts

Orca helps customers find assets running vulnerable OpenSSH versions and see each one’s exposure in context: whether it is reachable from the internet, at runtime, and how critical it is. Teams can use that context to fix the riskiest hosts first. Affected assets appear directly in the newItem view, so security teams can start with the most critical ones.

articles.title: Who Holds the Keys to Your ChatGPT Workspace?
articles.context: Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal...
articles.full_text:
Picture a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace a year after rollout. The IT lead who bought the licenses is still an Owner. So are the two admins she added during a busy week, and the director who asked for access “just to check something.” A contractor who left in the spring still has an account, because he was added by hand instead of through the identity provider. And a service account someone set up to run Codex jobs has a credential that never expires.

None of this is unusual. It’s what happens when a tool goes from pilot to every department in a few months, and nobody’s job is to keep an eye on the admin console.

Most of the security conversation around ChatGPT is about what people paste into it, and that’s fair. OpenAI’s Compliance Platform lets DLP and data security tools read conversations. But a more basic question usually goes unanswered: who actually holds the keys to the workspace?

ChatGPT Enterprise falls between teams, so each one assumes someone else is watching it:

Identity teams own the identity provider, but SCIM provisioning to ChatGPT is optional. Anyone added directly in the admin console never shows up in their access reviews.

Cloud security teams own AWS, Azure, and GCP. A ChatGPT workspace isn’t a cloud account, so their CNAPP never sees it.

The workspace owner is usually whoever bought the licenses. Owner access gets handed out to get things done, and it rarely gets taken back.

Rolling out an enterprise AI platform is still the right call. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action, up 4x in a year, and a sanctioned tool is the best way to get people off personal accounts. But someone still has to check how that tool is set up.

A service-account credential with no expiration date

A user not provisioned through the identity provider

Users added by hand skip your joiner-mover-leaver process, so offboarding may never reach them

A group with no members

ChatGPT belongs next to the rest of your risk

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security brings those parts into one platform. ChatGPT Enterprise sits next to Claude Enterprise at the model layer, alongside Vercel and your AWS, Azure, and GCP accounts.

articles.title: CVE-2026-101767: Critical Oracle EBS SQL Injection Actively Probed in the Wild
articles.context: CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3
articles.full_text:
What is CVE-2026-101767?

A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-101767, CVSS 9.8) was disclosed affecting Oracle E-Business Suite’s Application Object Library, allowing attackers to achieve full remote code execution and system takeover via an unauthenticated SQL injection in the Thin Client Framework servlet. Due to the potential for complete compromise of financial, payroll, and HR data managed by EBS, immediate patching is required.

How the Oracle EBS SQL injection leads to remote code execution

The issue originates from the Application Object Library’s TCF servlet at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, where missing authentication on a critical function combined with improper input sanitization leads to SQL injection as the privileged APPS database user. By sending specially crafted POST requests to the servlet instantiating oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer, attackers can execute arbitrary SQL commands and chain to operating system command execution as the EBS application account, potentially achieving full takeover of the EBS instance and all data it manages. No authentication is required to exploit this issue.

CVE-2026-101767 disclosure and exploitation timeline

The vulnerability was discovered by Horizon3.ai and reported to Oracle on July 24, 2026. Oracle addressed it in the October 2026 Critical Patch Update, released October 20. Within a week of the patch release, threat intelligence firm Defused observed exploratory exploitation attempts hitting Oracle EBS honeypots on October 27. EBS has historically been a target for financially motivated threat actors, including the Cl0p group’s large-scale EBS campaign the previous year.

Which Oracle E-Business Suite versions are affected?

The following components are affected: Oracle E-Business Suite Application Object Library, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle notes that earlier unsupported versions are likely also affected. The vulnerable servlet passes through the default EBS URL firewall configuration, meaning any internet-facing EBS instance with default settings is exposed. Organizations running EBS for financial, payroll, HR, and procurement operations face elevated risk due to the sensitive data accessible through the APPS database user.

How to patch and mitigate CVE-2026-101767

Users should apply the October 2026 Critical Patch Update immediately (details in My Oracle Support Note KA923), and also patch the underlying EBS Database and Fusion Middleware components, which have separate CPU entries. As interim mitigations until patching is complete, administrators should remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restrict network access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks only.

Is CVE-2026-101767 being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, Horizon3.ai has published technical details of the attack chain, and active probing has been confirmed in the wild by Defused. The vulnerability is not yet listed on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments.

What attackers can do with a compromised Oracle EBS instance

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary SQL and OS commands as the APPS and EBS application accounts, exfiltrate or manipulate sensitive financial, payroll, and HR data, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or full infrastructure compromise.

How Orca helps find and prioritize vulnerable Oracle EBS assets

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable versions of Oracle E-Business Suite, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the newItem view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first

articles.title: Securing Vercel at Scale: From One Team to Every Team
articles.context: Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget)
articles.full_text:
On Thursday, a customer marketing manager vibe codes a community portal where customers can sign in, post questions, and search past answers. By Friday it’s live on Vercel, with a custom domain, an OPENAI_API_KEY for the AI search saved as a plain config variable, and a database full of customer names, emails, and support threads.

No ticket. No code review. No security sign-off. Nothing broke, so nobody looked.

Vercel has the settings to prevent every part of that. The harder question belongs to the security team: how do you know those settings are on, for every team, across the whole company?

The builder population just changed

Vercel used to be where front-end engineers shipped Next.js apps. Now it’s where AI ships apps for everyone else. Vercel’s v0 has crossed 4 million users (SaaStr), and CEO Guillermo Rauch says more than 60% of activity on Vercel is now driven by coding agents (The Stack).

Many of those apps belong to companies, not hobbyists. Researchers at Red Access found about 5,000 corporate apps among 380,000 public assets on AI app platforms, and about 40% of those exposed sensitive data (TechTarget).

Why your current tools only see part of it

Vercel isn’t a cloud account, a repo, or a typical SaaS app. It’s a control plane that sits between all three, so each tool you already own sees only part of it:

CNAPP sees the AWS, Azure, or GCP accounts DevOps provisioned. Vercel isn’t one of them.

AppSec scans the repos you point it at. An app built from a prompt may never pass through one.

SSPM checks SaaS sign-in and access settings, but rarely Vercel’s deployment and firewall settings.

Vercel’s own Security Dashboard, free on every plan since August 2026, is the best place to start. It scores a team on settings like MFA, owner count, token expiry, and secret storage (Vercel). But it covers one team at a time, a fixed list of checks, and only Vercel.

These settings are configured in Vercel, team by team, usually by whoever created the team: access tokens, environment variables, custom domains, deployment protection, SAML enforcement, firewall rules. That person usually isn’t on the security team.

Vercel’s dashboard tells one team how its settings look. Security teams need every team, more checks, and one place to work them next to the rest of their risk.

What Orca adds beyond Vercel’s dashboard

The integration supports Vercel Enterprise. You connect it with a Full Account access token created by a dedicated service user with the Enterprise Viewer and Security roles, so Orca’s access stays read-only. Set an expiration on the token and rotate it (Vercel access tokens). If your organization enforces SAML, connect each team with its own team token instead. There’s no agent to install, nothing to deploy in Vercel, and no change to how anyone builds.

Orca inventories every team the token can reach, including teams added later: projects, deployments, domains, members, access tokens, firewall settings, and environment-variable metadata, never the values. Each Vercel team shows up as an account in Orca, so you see every team in one place instead of one dashboard per team.

Orca runs a variety of detections out of the box. Some overlap with Vercel’s dashboard.

Area

SAML configured but not enforced, invitations pending more than 14 days

Members without MFA, tokens with no expiration, too many owners, long-lived credentials that could use OIDC

Production deployments without protection, custom firewall (WAF) disabled, no bot blocking, no IP blocking rules, overly permissive bypass rules

Four misconfigurations that AI-built apps make by default

These four issues come up most with AI-built apps. None is a mistake anyone makes on purpose. Each is a default, or a step builders skip because nothing breaks without it.

Production URLs with no login. Vercel’s Deployment Protection covers preview URLs by default. Production is a separate setting. Builders rarely change it, because the app works fine either way. The result is a public, indexable production URL with nothing in front of it. The fix is free: since September 2026, every plan can put Vercel Authentication in front of production and make it the team default (Vercel).

Secrets saved as readable Config variables. Since August 2026, Vercel stores each variable as Config (readable) or Secret (write-only) (Vercel). Values are encrypted at rest, but a STRIPE_SECRET_KEY saved as Config stays readable to anyone with project access. The name is the giveaway, and that’s what Orca flags.

SAML connected but not enforced. The identity team links the IdP to Vercel. Nobody turns on enforcement, so members can still reach the team without a SAML session (Vercel).

Long-lived and forgotten access tokens. A Full Account or Team token carries the role of the person who created it. Tokens set to never expire, or unused for 90 days, are standing credentials nobody is watching. Orca flags both. Project-scoped tokens limit any one token to a single project (Vercel).

One queue for every team

A dashboard per Vercel team works for the person who owns that team. It doesn’t work for a security team responsible for dozens of them.

In Orca, Vercel findings show up alongside your AWS, Azure, and GCP findings, in the same risk scoring, alert workflows, and ticketing integrations your team already uses. Each finding shows which Vercel team owns the project, so it reaches someone who can fix it. New teams are covered as soon as they’re created, without anyone registering them.

Vercel findings land prioritized in the same queue as your cloud findings in the Orca Platform

Vercel is one part of the AI-built app

An AI-built app has five parts: the model behind it, the agent or builder that made it, the platform it runs on, the database and login behind it, and the cloud account under it. Each comes from a different vendor and has a different owner. None of those owners is security.

Orca AI AppGen Security covers these parts in one platform instead of one tool per vendor. Today that means Vercel, where AI-built apps run, and Claude Enterprise, where many of them start, in the same inventory and the same queue. More platforms are coming.

The goal isn’t to slow builders down. They keep the tools they picked. Security gets enough visibility to say yes instead of no.

articles.title: Node.js Brotli Decoder Out-of-Bounds Write Threatens Remote Code Execution Across All Supported Versions
articles.context: No authentication is required to exploit this issue when the target processes attacker-controlled compressed data
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary:

A high-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) was disclosed affecting Node.js across all supported release lines (22.x, 24.x, 26.x), allowing attackers to achieve remote code execution via malformed Brotli-compressed data processed by node:zlib or fetch(). Due to the potential for crashes, memory disclosure, and code execution in cloud workloads, immediate patching is required.

About CVE-2026-111497

The issue originates from the bundled Brotli decompression library, where an invalid block switch declaring only one block type is not properly rejected, leading to an out-of-bounds write past the decoder buffer boundary. By sending specially crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP responses or request bodies, attackers can trigger memory corruption and crash target applications, potentially achieving remote code execution. No authentication is required to exploit this issue when the target processes attacker-controlled compressed data.

Affected Systems

The following components are affected: the Brotli decoder bundled in Node.js, exposed through node:zlib decompression APIs and the built-in fetch() function when handling Brotli-compressed HTTP responses (Content-Encoding: br). Node.js versions prior to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 are vulnerable, as are upstream Brotli library versions prior to 1.2.1, 1.1.1, and 1.0.10. Node.js 20.x and earlier have reached end-of-life and will not receive patches. Any application decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data is at risk, including cloud workloads, serverless functions, and container images running unpatched Node.js.

The same security release also addresses three additional high-severity issues. CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483 allow TLS hostname verification bypass via non-canonical IP address formats (octal, fullwidth digits) that circumvent tls.checkServerIdentity() checks. CVE-2026-105482 is a DNS resolver flaw where embedded NUL bytes truncate domain names, enabling resolution of attacker-chosen domains. In total, the release fixes 10 vulnerabilities: four High, three Medium, and three Low severity.

Remediation

Users should upgrade immediately to Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, and rebuild container images on patched base images. There is no reliable in-app workaround for the Brotli flaw; setting Accept-Encoding: identity does not prevent fetch() from decompressing Brotli responses. Node.js 20.x users must migrate to a supported release line. For the TLS issues, an interim mitigation is to reject hosts where net.isIP(host) returns 0 but net.isIP(url.domainToASCII(host)) returns non-zero. For the DNS issue, reject names containing NUL characters before passing them to dns.resolve functions.

Risk Impact

At the time of writing, a public proof-of-concept published on October 22 achieved code execution only on a deliberately weakened test build; on standard production builds it caused a crash and limited memory read. No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. Regardless, the severity and ease of exploitation make this vulnerability high risk, especially in internet-facing deployments where applications process Brotli-compressed data from untrusted sources.

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to crash Node.js processes and cause denial of service, read sensitive memory contents from the application, and potentially achieve full remote code execution, leading to service disruption, data exposure, or infrastructure compromise across cloud environments.How Orca Can Help

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable Node.js versions, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly in the alert view, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first.
